data: Fragment of a painted Greek inscription

A fragment of a block of the local soft white limestone, with the surface finished and then red letters painted directly onto the stone. Intact on the right side, broken on the left and below, and perhaps incomplete at the top (the top appears to be worked and finished, perhaps to receive another block above). Modern plaster suppport added to the base. The rear is uneven and curves and is only roughly finished.
whitish soft calcarenite with orangish patina, likely calcarenite degli Iblei (sand-grade limestone) (identification based on pXRF)
Traces of five lines of letters, vacat at the end of line 1.

Finely painted Hellenistic letters in rigid style without serfis. Alpha has straight bar; epsilon has short middle bar; omicron is small and above the line (14-17 mm); omega is small, circular, closed, and almost sits on the line (19 mm).
Found in excavations in the area of the 'Foro Romano' (i.e. Piazza d'Armi) in 1888. Now in storage in the archaeological museum, magazzino B, cass.20
I.Sicily with the permission of the Assessorato Regionale dei Beni Culturali e dell’Identità Siciliana - Dipartimento dei Beni Culturali e dell’Identità Siciliana; photo J. Prag 2021-11-12

An outstanding collection of archaeological material. The collection ranges from Siracusa and the surrounding territory (Megara Hyblaia, Akrai, Kasmenai etc) to encompass all of eastern Sicily, reaching as far as Gela and Agrigento. The ground floor covers prehistory through to the end of the Classical period. Upstairs includes Hellenistic and Roman Syracuse and a display of material from the catacombs. A gallery displaying material from Hellenistic eastern Sicily is in preparation.

translation

commentary

Orsi declined to speculate on the nature of the text in his original publication. Kaibel suggested that the fragment was part of a funerary verse epigram, a view which Manganaro merely repeated without reviewing the text in 1994. In 1999 instead, he suggested that this might be a fragment of an honorific text for a teacher of the youth of the gymnasium, and although his restorations are excessively speculative, the core points that we would seem to have the words καιρὸν, a form of the participle παιδευόμενος (the sequence of letters can hardly be restored as anything else), and a reference to ἀρετή, very strongly favour the suggestion. The vacats after lines 1 and 5 encourage the view that the right margin of the stone is preserved. The ΤΩΝ at the start of line 1 are perhaps more likely to be the end of a genitive plural, rather than the article, given the vacat. The survival of a high quality painted text from the Hellenistic period is unusual, but especially given the relatively poor quality of the local stone for epigraphic carving, perhaps should not be surprising.
